title: Σαρπηδὼν καὶ Γλαῦκος
about: Stones fly thick as snowflakes from both sides, and Zeus rouses his son Sarpedon, who goes at the wall like a hungry lion at a sheepfold. He speaks to Glaucus: they are honoured in Lycia with seats, meat, cups and land, so they must stand among the foremost; if war could make them ageless and immortal he would stay out of it, but since death waits for every man they should go and either win glory or give it to another. They lead the Lycians against the tower of Menestheus, who shudders at the sight and looks along the wall for help. He sees the two Ajaxes and Teucer but cannot be heard over the din, so he sends the herald Thoötes to call them, both if possible, or at least Telamonian Ajax with Teucer. Ajax leaves the son of Oileus and Lycomedes to rally the Danaans and goes with Teucer, whose bow Pandion carries; they reach the tower just as the Lycian leaders climb onto the battlements, and the two sides close in battle.

sentences.t: ὣς τώ γε προβοῶντε μάχην ὄτρυνον Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: So those two, shouting forth, were urging the fighting of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: So the two of them, calling out loud, urged on the Achaeans’ fighting.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual ‘those two’, the two Ajaxes of the last part, and the dual runs through the line: προβοῶντε is the dual participle of προβοάω ‘shout aloud’ (whether the prefix means ‘aloud’ or ‘in front’ is not clear). ὄτρυνον is the imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, without augment. μάχην is the thing urged and Ἀχαιῶν the men whose fight it is, ‘the Achaeans’ fighting’.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’, ὥς τε νιφάδες χιόνος πίπτωσι θαμειαὶ
ἤματι χειμερίῳ, ὅτε τ’ ὤρετο μητίετα Ζεὺς
νιφέμεν ἀνθρώποισι πιφαυσκόμενος τὰ ἃ κῆλα·
sentences.i: As thick flakes of snow fall on a wintry day, when Zeus the counsellor has set himself to snow on men and show them his own shafts;
sentences.n: A long simile begins here, and its main clause waits until line 287, where ὣς τῶν picks up the opening τῶν δ’ ‘and of them’. ὥς τε νιφάδες … πίπτωσι is a comparison with the subjunctive, ‘as flakes fall’. ὤρετο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, and with the infinitive νιφέμεν (νίφω ‘snow’, epic ending -έμεν) it means ‘has set himself to snow’. τὰ ἃ is the article with the possessive ὅς ‘his own’, not the relative; κῆλα are ‘shafts’, as in the god’s shafts of 1.53, so the snowflakes are weapons Zeus is making known to men. μητίετα Ζεύς is the stock ‘counsellor Zeus’.

sentences.t:
κοιμήσας δ’ ἀνέμους χέει ἔμπεδον, ὄφρα καλύψῃ
ὑψηλῶν ὀρέων κορυφὰς καὶ πρώονας ἄκρους
καὶ πεδία λωτοῦντα καὶ ἀνδρῶν πίονα ἔργα,
sentences.l:
and having lulled the winds to sleep, he pours steadily, until it covers
the peaks of high mountains and the spurs, the high ones,
and the lotus-growing plains and the rich farmlands of men,
sentences.i: he lulls the winds to sleep and pours the snow down steadily, until it has covered the peaks of the high mountains, the high spurs, the lotus-growing plains and the rich farmlands of men,
sentences.n: The subject is still Zeus. κοιμήσας is the aorist participle of κοιμάω ‘lull to sleep’; χέει ‘pours’ has no stated object, and the snow is meant. ἔμπεδον is an adverb, ‘steadily’. ὄφρα καλύψῃ is ‘until it covers’, with the subjunctive. πρώονας ἄκρους: a πρών is a jutting piece of high ground, ‘spur’ here (kept apart from the ἀκταί ‘headlands’ of line 284), and ἄκρους is ‘high’. λωτοῦντα is a contracted form of λωτόεντα, ‘abounding in lotus’ (the fodder plant), and ἔργα ‘works’ are the tilled farmlands.

sentences.t:
καί τ’ ἐφ’ ἁλὸς πολιῆς κέχυται λιμέσιν τε καὶ ἀκταῖς,
κῦμα δέ μιν προσπλάζον ἐρύκεται·
sentences.l:
and over the grey sea it is poured out, over harbours and headlands,
and the wave, washing up against it, holds it back;
sentences.i: and it is poured out over the grey sea too, over the harbours and headlands, and the wave, as it washes up against it, holds it back;
sentences.n: καί τ’ ἐφ’ ἁλὸς πολιῆς: ἐφ’ ἁλὸς πολιῆς is ‘over the grey sea’ (ἐπί with the genitive); the datives λιμέσιν ‘harbours’ and ἀκταῖς ‘headlands’ say where else it lies, with ἐπί understood again. κέχυται is the perfect passive of χέω ‘has been poured’, and the snow is its subject. In κῦμα … ἐρύκεται the subject is the wave (κῦμα) and μιν is the snow; ἐρύκεται is middle in form but active in sense, ‘holds back’. προσπλάζον is the neuter participle ‘washing up against’, agreeing with κῦμα.

sentences.t:
ἄλλά τε πάντα
εἴλυται καθύπερθ’, ὅτ’ ἐπιβρίσῃ Διὸς ὄμβρος·
sentences.l:
and all other things
are wrapped over from above, when the rain of Zeus bears down heavily;
sentences.i: and everything else is wrapped over from above, when the rain of Zeus bears down heavily;
sentences.n: ἄλλά τε πάντα is ‘and all other things’, neuter plural, set against the sea’s edge just described. εἴλυται is the perfect passive of εἰλύω ‘wrap round’; καθύπερθ’ is ‘from above’. The half-line ὅτ’ ἐπιβρίσῃ Διὸς ὄμβρος is word for word one that closes a simile of a flooded river at 5.91, and its English is kept; there the ‘rain of Zeus’ is a downpour; here the same words stand in a snowstorm.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῶν ἀμφοτέρωσε λίθοι πωτῶντο θαμειαί,
αἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐς Τρῶας, αἱ δ’ ἐκ Τρώων ἐς Ἀχαιούς,
βαλλομένων·
sentences.i: So the stones flew thick in both directions, some at the Trojans and others from the Trojans at the Achaeans, as the men were pelted;
sentences.n: ὣς τῶν answers the simile’s opening τῶν δ’ (278): ‘so of them’. ἀμφοτέρωσε ‘to both sides’ has the suffix -σε of direction. πωτῶντο is the imperfect of ποτάομαι ‘fly about’ in its epic form. λίθοι is the subject, but θαμειαί ‘thick’ and αἱ μὲν … αἱ δ’ ‘some … others’ are feminine, which is a rare feminine use of λίθος. βαλλομένων, the genitive plural ‘being pelted’, agrees with the τῶν of ὣς τῶν.

sentences.t: τὸ δὲ τεῖχος ὕπερ πᾶν δοῦπος ὀρώρει.
sentences.l: and over the wall, all of it, a thud had arisen.
sentences.i: and a thud had risen over the whole wall.
sentences.n: ὕπερ follows its noun (so the accent falls on the first syllable) and means ‘over’; πᾶν agrees with τεῖχος, so ‘over the whole wall’. δοῦπος is a ‘thud’, a heavy dull sound. ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι ‘had arisen’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄν πω τότε γε Τρῶες καὶ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
τείχεος ἐρρήξαντο πύλας καὶ μακρὸν ὀχῆα,
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ υἱὸν ἑὸν Σαρπηδόνα μητίετα Ζεὺς
ὦρσεν ἐπ’ Ἀργείοισι λέονθ’ ὣς βουσὶν ἕλιξιν.
sentences.l:
Not even yet then would the Trojans and glorious Hector
have broken the gates of the wall and the long bar,
if counsellor Zeus had not then roused his own son Sarpedon
against the Argives, like a lion against crumple-horned cattle.
sentences.i: Even then the Trojans and glorious Hector would not yet have broken the gates of the wall and its long bar, if Zeus the counsellor had not roused his own son Sarpedon against the Argives, like a lion against cattle of crumpled horn.
sentences.n: This is a past unreal condition: οὐδ’ ἄν … ἐρρήξαντο ‘would not have broken’ (aorist with ἄν), εἰ μὴ … ὦρσεν ‘if he had not roused’. ἐρρήξαντο is the aorist middle of ῥήγνυμι, and τείχεος (epic genitive, Attic τείχους) depends on πύλας; ὀχῆα, from ὀχεύς, is ‘the long bar’ of the gates. φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ and μητίετα Ζεύς are stock epithets, ‘glorious’ and ‘counsellor’. ἑόν is the possessive ‘his own’. λέονθ’ ὣς is λέοντα ὥς ‘like a lion’, and ἕλιξιν is the dative plural of ἕλιξ ‘twisting’, ‘crumple-horned’ as in the Odyssey; whether the word speaks of the horns or of the gait is not certain.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἀσπίδα μὲν πρόσθ’ ἔσχετο πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην
καλὴν χαλκείην ἐξήλατον, ἣν ἄρα χαλκεὺς
ἤλασεν, ἔντοσθεν δὲ βοείας ῥάψε θαμειὰς
χρυσείῃς ῥάβδοισι διηνεκέσιν περὶ κύκλον.
sentences.l:
At once, his shield, in front he held, equal on every side,
fine, of bronze, beaten out, which then a smith
beat out, and within oxhides he stitched, thick ones,
with golden rods, unbroken, round the circle.
sentences.i: At once he held his shield before him, a fine one of bronze, equal on every side and beaten out, which a smith had hammered; inside it he had stitched thick oxhides, with golden rods running unbroken round the circle.
sentences.n: The subject is Sarpedon. ἔσχετο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘held before himself’, and πρόσθ’ is ‘in front’. πάντοσ’ is πάντοσε ‘on every side’; ἐΐσην agrees with ἀσπίδα, and πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην is the fixed phrase ‘equal on every side’, probably meaning evenly round. ἐξήλατον ‘beaten out’ and ἤλασεν (from ἐλαύνω) ‘beat out’ describe the smith’s work, and the smith is also the subject of ῥάψε, ‘stitched’ (ῥάπτω, without augment). βοείας is an adjective used as a noun, ‘oxhides’. χρυσείῃς is the dative plural with the epic ending -ῃς (Attic -αῖς). The ῥάβδοισι ‘rods’ run διηνεκέσιν ‘without a break’ round the κύκλος, the shield’s circle; the Greek does not say what they were for.

sentences.t:
τὴν ἄρ’ ὅ γε πρόσθε σχόμενος δύο δοῦρε τινάσσων
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ὥς τε λέων ὀρεσίτροφος, ὅς τ’ ἐπιδευὴς
δηρὸν ἔῃ κρειῶν, κέλεται δέ ἑ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
μήλων πειρήσοντα καὶ ἐς πυκινὸν δόμον ἐλθεῖν·
sentences.l:
That then he, holding it before him, brandishing two spears,
set out to go like a mountain-nurtured lion, who, lacking
for long may be, of meats, and bids him his manly spirit
to make trial of the flocks, and to go even into a solid house;
sentences.i: Holding it before him and brandishing two spears, he set out like a mountain-nurtured lion that has long been lacking in meat, and his proud spirit bids him make trial of the flocks and go even into a solid house;
sentences.n: τὴν is the shield. σχόμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἔχω ‘holding before him’, and δοῦρε is the dual of δόρυ ‘spear’. The simile of the lion begins: βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ὥς τε λέων ὀρεσίτροφος differs by one particle from an Odyssey half-line (βῆ δ’ ἴμεν …), and its English is kept. ἐπιδευής ‘lacking’ takes the genitive κρειῶν ‘meats’, and ἔῃ is the subjunctive of εἰμί, ‘may be’, as in general comparisons. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is the stock ‘manly spirit’ (‘proud spirit’ in the loose English). πειρήσοντα is a future participle, accusative, agreeing with ἑ ‘him’: ‘to make trial’. Line 301 is word for word a line of the Odyssey, where the lion’s belly bids him instead, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ χ’ εὕρῃσι παρ’ αὐτόφι βώτορας ἄνδρας
σὺν κυσὶ καὶ δούρεσσι φυλάσσοντας περὶ μῆλα,
sentences.l:
For even if he finds on the spot herdsmen
with dogs and spears guarding around the flocks,
sentences.i: For even if he finds herdsmen right there, guarding the flocks with dogs and spears,
sentences.n: εἴ περ γάρ χ’ is ‘for even if’, with χ’ for κε before a rough breathing; the subjunctive εὕρῃσι opens a general statement that 304 completes. παρ’ αὐτόφι ‘right at hand’ has the old ending -φι. βώτορας ἄνδρας is ‘herdsmen’ (βώτωρ is the herdsman; ἄνδρας is not translated again). φυλάσσοντας ‘guarding’ agrees with them. κυσί is the dative plural of κύων ‘dog’, and δούρεσσι the epic dative plural of δόρυ ‘spear’.

sentences.t:
οὔ ῥά τ’ ἀπείρητος μέμονε σταθμοῖο δίεσθαι,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἄρ’ ἢ ἥρπαξε μετάλμενος, ἠὲ καὶ αὐτὸς
ἔβλητ’ ἐν πρώτοισι θοῆς ἀπὸ χειρὸς ἄκοντι·
sentences.i: he is not minded to be driven off from the steading without making trial; no, either he leaps in and snatches one, or he himself is struck among the foremost by a javelin from a swift hand;
sentences.n: The lion is still the subject. ἀπείρητος ‘untried’ picks up πειρήσοντα above: he does not turn back without making a trial. μέμονε is the perfect of μέμονα ‘is minded’, with the infinitive δίεσθαι; the sense ‘to be driven off’ is the usual one, taken from the context and not certain (the infinitive is middle in form), with σταθμοῖο, the genitive of σταθμός, ‘from the steading’. ἢ ἥρπαξε … ἠέ … ἔβλητ’ are ‘either … or’ with aorists that state what always happens; μετάλμενος is the aorist participle of μεθάλλομαι ‘leap upon’, and ἥρπαξε has no stated object. ἔβλητ’ is ἔβλητο, ‘is struck’.

sentences.t:
ὥς ῥα τότ’ ἀντίθεον Σαρπηδόνα θυμὸς ἀνῆκε
τεῖχος ἐπαΐξαι διά τε ῥήξασθαι ἐπάλξεις.
sentences.l:
So then at that time godlike Sarpedon his spirit urged on
to rush upon the wall and to break through the battlements.
sentences.i: So his spirit urged godlike Sarpedon on to rush at the wall and break through the battlements.
sentences.n: ὥς ῥα τότ’ closes the simile of the lion. ἀντίθεος, here ‘godlike’, is Sarpedon’s stock epithet. θυμός ‘spirit’ is the subject of ἀνῆκε, the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘urge on’, which takes the accusative and an infinitive. ἐπαΐξαι (‘to rush at’) takes τεῖχος; διά τε ῥήξασθαι is διαρρήξασθαι split by tmesis, ‘to break through’, with ἐπάλξεις, the screens along the top of the wall.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δὲ Γλαῦκον προσέφη παῖδ’ Ἱππολόχοιο·
sentences.l: And at once Glaucus he addressed, Hippolochus’ son:
sentences.i: And at once he spoke to Glaucus, the son of Hippolochus:
sentences.n: The speaker is Sarpedon, still the subject. προσέφη is the aorist of προσφημί ‘address’, with Γλαῦκον as object; παῖδ’ Ἱππολόχοιο is ‘son of Hippolochus’. Glaucus is the second of the Lycian commanders.

sentences.t:
Γλαῦκε τί ἢ δὴ νῶϊ τετιμήμεσθα μάλιστα
ἕδρῃ τε κρέασίν τε ἰδὲ πλείοις δεπάεσσιν
ἐν Λυκίῃ, πάντες δὲ θεοὺς ὣς εἰσορόωσι,
sentences.l:
“Glaucus, why indeed have we two been honoured most
with a seat, and with meats, and with full cups
in Lycia, and all look at us as at gods,
sentences.i: “Glaucus, why are we two honoured most of all in Lycia, with a seat, with meats, and with full cups, while all look on us as on gods,
sentences.n: Sarpedon’s speech opens with a question about honour and what it costs, and the question runs on for two units. τετιμήμεσθα is the perfect passive of τιμάω, ‘we have been honoured’, and νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’. ἕδρῃ τε κρέασίν τε ἰδὲ πλείοις δεπάεσσιν is a line (8.162) spoken to Diomedes by Hector, and its English is kept; δεπάεσσιν is the epic dative plural of δέπας ‘cup’. θεοὺς ὣς is ‘as (at) gods’, with ὥς after its noun; εἰσορόωσι is the uncontracted form of εἰσοράω ‘look at’, and ‘us’ is not stated.

sentences.t:
καὶ τέμενος νεμόμεσθα μέγα Ξάνθοιο παρ’ ὄχθας
καλὸν φυταλιῆς καὶ ἀρούρης πυροφόροιο;
sentences.l:
and we occupy a great precinct beside the banks of Xanthus,
fine, of planted land and of wheat-bearing plough-land?
sentences.i: and hold a great estate beside the banks of the Xanthus, a fine one of planted land and wheat-bearing plough-land?
sentences.n: νεμόμεσθα is the present of νέμομαι ‘occupy’. τέμενος is a plot of land set apart for a lord (‘precinct’ in l, ‘estate’ in i). Ξάνθοιο is the genitive of Ξάνθος, the river of Lycia, and ὄχθας is the accusative plural of ὄχθη ‘bank’. καλὸν φυταλιῆς καὶ ἀρούρης (‘fine, of planted land and of plough-land’) is the phrase used of Bellerophon’s estate at 6.195, and its English is kept; πυροφόροιο ‘wheat-bearing’ (πυρός ‘wheat’) agrees with ἀρούρης and is new.

sentences.t:
τὼ νῦν χρὴ Λυκίοισι μέτα πρώτοισιν ἐόντας
ἑστάμεν ἠδὲ μάχης καυστείρης ἀντιβολῆσαι,
ὄφρά τις ὧδ’ εἴπῃ Λυκίων πύκα θωρηκτάων·
sentences.l:
Therefore now it is necessary, among the foremost Lycians being,
to stand, and to encounter the burning battle,
so that some one of the Lycians, closely corseleted, may say thus:
sentences.i: And so now we must stand among the foremost Lycians and meet the burning battle, so that one of the closely corseleted Lycians may say:
sentences.n: τὼ is τῷ ‘therefore’. χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the accusative ἐόντας ‘(us) being’, with the infinitives ἑστάμεν ‘to stand’ and ἀντιβολῆσαι ‘to meet’; μέτα is μετά ‘among’, with the accent drawn back. The second line is also found at 4.342, and its English is kept. ὄφρά τις … εἴπῃ is ‘so that someone may say’, with the subjunctive. θωρηκτάων is the genitive plural of θωρηκτής, ‘one who wears a corselet’; πύκα is ‘closely, thickly’, and whether it speaks of the fit of the corselets or their strength is not known.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰν ἀκλεέες Λυκίην κάτα κοιρανέουσιν
ἡμέτεροι βασιλῆες, ἔδουσί τε πίονα μῆλα
οἶνόν τ’ ἔξαιτον μελιηδέα· ἀλλ’ ἄρα καὶ ἲς
ἐσθλή, ἐπεὶ Λυκίοισι μέτα πρώτοισι μάχονται.
sentences.l:
‘Truly not without glory throughout Lycia act as rulers
our kings, and they eat the fat flocks
and wine, choice, honey-sweet; but then also strength
is good, since among the foremost Lycians they fight.’
sentences.i: ‘It is not without glory that our kings rule throughout Lycia: they eat the fat flocks and drink choice honey-sweet wine; and indeed their strength is good too, since they fight among the foremost Lycians.’
sentences.n: These are the words Sarpedon imagines a Lycian saying, so the single quotation marks stand inside his speech. οὐ μὰν ἀκλεέες is ‘truly not without glory’, a way of saying ‘gloriously’. Λυκίην κάτα is κατὰ Λυκίην ‘throughout Lycia’, with the preposition after its noun. κοιρανέουσιν (from κοίρανος ‘ruler’) is ‘act as rulers’, with no swagger in it here. ἔδουσι is from ἔδω, the epic by-form of ἐσθίω ‘eat’, and ‘drink’ is supplied for the wine. ἔξαιτον is ‘picked out’, so ‘choice’ (from ἐξαιτέω). ἲς is ‘strength’, ἐσθλή ‘good’. The last line echoes line 315.

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπον εἰ μὲν γὰρ πόλεμον περὶ τόνδε φυγόντε
αἰεὶ δὴ μέλλοιμεν ἀγήρω τ’ ἀθανάτω τε
ἔσσεσθ’, οὔτέ κεν αὐτὸς ἐνὶ πρώτοισι μαχοίμην
οὔτέ κε σὲ στέλλοιμι μάχην ἐς κυδιάνειραν·
sentences.l:
O good one, for if indeed about this war, we two having escaped,
forever we were going, ageless and immortal,
to be, neither would I myself among the foremost fight,
nor would I send you into the man-glorifying battle;
sentences.i: My good fellow, if we two, once we had escaped this war, were going to be ageless and immortal for ever, I would neither fight myself among the foremost nor send you into the battle that brings men glory;
sentences.n: The speech turns from the Lycians’ praise to Sarpedon’s reason, and γάρ ties it back to the question. ὦ πέπον is a friendly address; the meaning of πέπον is not known, and the usual rendering is kept. The condition is εἰ … μέλλοιμεν (optative) ‘if we were going to be’, and the answer is two optatives with κε, ‘I would fight’, ‘I would send’. φυγόντε is the dual aorist participle ‘we two having escaped’; περὶ … τόνδε with φυγόντε is unusual, and the sense is ‘having got clear of this war’. ἀγήρω τ’ ἀθανάτω τε is the dual ‘ageless and immortal’, and ἔσσεσθ’ is ἔσεσθαι, the future infinitive of εἰμί. κυδιάνειραν ‘man-glorifying’ (κῦδος + ἀνήρ) agrees with μάχην.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἔμπης γὰρ κῆρες ἐφεστᾶσιν θανάτοιο
μυρίαι, ἃς οὐκ ἔστι φυγεῖν βροτὸν οὐδ’ ὑπαλύξαι,
ἴομεν ἠέ τῳ εὖχος ὀρέξομεν ἠέ τις ἡμῖν.
sentences.l:
But now, for in any case death-spirits of death stand over us,
countless, which it is not possible for a mortal to flee or escape,
let us go, either to someone we shall reach out a boast, or someone to us.”
sentences.i: But as it is, countless spirits of death stand over us all the same, and no mortal can flee or escape them; so let us go, and either we shall give a triumph to someone, or someone will give one to us.”
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ‘but as things are’ sets the hard fact against the wish of the last unit. ἔμπης is ‘all the same, in any case’. ἐφεστᾶσιν is the perfect of ἐφίστημι ‘stand over’, and κῆρες θανάτοιο are the death-spirits, μυρίαι ‘countless’; ἅς is the object of both φυγεῖν and ὑπαλύξαι, and ἔστι means ‘it is possible’, with βροτόν as the accusative subject of the infinitives. ἴομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive ‘let us go’. εὖχος ὀρέξομεν is ‘we shall reach out a boast’, the future of ὀρέγω, and the verb is understood again with ἠέ τις ἡμῖν, ‘or someone (will reach it out) to us’; the boast is the glory of the man who kills the other. This closes Sarpedon’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδὲ Γλαῦκος ἀπετράπετ’ οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Glaucus did not turn away, nor disobey;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Glaucus neither turned away nor disobeyed;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is the stock ‘so he spoke’. ἀπετράπετ’ is ἀπετράπετο, the aorist middle of ἀποτρέπω, ‘turned himself away’, and ἀπίθησε (ἀπιθέω, the opposite of ‘obey’) has no augment. The line is the usual ‘did not disobey’ pattern, with Glaucus as its subject.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ ἰθὺς βήτην Λυκίων μέγα ἔθνος ἄγοντε.
sentences.l: And those two went straight on, of the Lycians a great band leading.
sentences.i: and the two went straight on, leading a great band of Lycians.
sentences.n: τὼ δ’ is the dual ‘and those two’ (Sarpedon and Glaucus). βήτην is the dual aorist of βαίνω ‘went’, without augment, and ἄγοντε the dual participle ‘leading’. ἰθύς is ‘straight’. ἔθνος is ‘band’, a body of people.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δὲ ἰδὼν ῥίγησ’ υἱὸς Πετεῶο Μενεσθεύς·
τοῦ γὰρ δὴ πρὸς πύργον ἴσαν κακότητα φέροντες.
sentences.l:
And them seeing, shuddered the son of Peteos, Menestheus;
for indeed toward his tower they were going, evil bringing.
sentences.i: Menestheus, the son of Peteos, shuddered at the sight of them, for they were coming to his tower, bringing misfortune.
sentences.n: τοὺς δὲ ἰδών is ‘and having seen them’, the Lycians. ῥίγησ’ is ῥίγησε, the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’, and the cause comes in the next line. Πετεῶο is the epic genitive of Πετεώς, ‘Peteos’ son’. τοῦ is the pronoun ‘his’, and ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘they were going’. κακότητα φέροντες is ‘bringing evil’, ‘misfortune’ in the loose English.

sentences.t:
πάπτηνεν δ’ ἀνὰ πύργον Ἀχαιῶν εἴ τιν’ ἴδοιτο
ἡγεμόνων, ὅς τίς οἱ ἀρὴν ἑτάροισιν ἀμύναι·
sentences.l:
And he looked about along the tower of the Achaeans, in case any he might see
of the leaders, who for his companions ruin might ward off;
sentences.i: He looked about along the tower of the Achaeans to see whether he could catch sight of any of the leaders who might ward off ruin for his companions;
sentences.n: πάπτηνεν is the aorist of παπταίνω ‘look about (anxiously)’. πύργον here is the stretch of wall with its tower, ‘the tower of the Achaeans’. εἴ τιν’ ἴδοιτο is εἰ with the optative, ‘in case he might see’, and ἡγεμόνων is the genitive ‘of leaders’ after τιν’. ὅς τίς … ἀμύναι is a relative clause with the optative of ἀμύνω, ‘one who might ward off’; οἱ is ‘for him’, ἑτάροισιν ‘for his companions’, and ἀρή is ‘ruin’.

sentences.t:
ἐς δ’ ἐνόησ’ Αἴαντε δύω πολέμου ἀκορήτω
ἑσταότας, Τεῦκρόν τε νέον κλισίηθεν ἰόντα
ἐγγύθεν·
sentences.i: And he caught sight of the two Ajaxes, who could never have enough of war, standing there, and of Teucer, who was just coming from his hut close by;
sentences.n: ἐς δ’ ἐνόησ’ is εἰσενόησε split by tmesis, ‘caught sight of’. Αἴαντε δύω is ‘the two Ajaxes’, the dual with δύω. πολέμου ἀκορήτω is the dual of ἀκόρητος ‘insatiate’ with the genitive ‘of war’. ἑσταότας is the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’. νέον is ‘newly’, κλισίηθεν ‘from the hut’ (-θεν), ἰόντα ‘coming’, and ἐγγύθεν ‘near at hand’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὔ πώς οἱ ἔην βώσαντι γεγωνεῖν·
sentences.l: but in no way was it for him, having shouted, to make himself heard;
sentences.i: but there was no way he could make himself heard by shouting;
sentences.n: οὔ πώς is ‘in no way’, and ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί, ‘was’. βώσαντι is the aorist participle of βοάω ‘shout’, in the dative with οἱ ‘for him’. γεγωνεῖν is ‘to make oneself heard’.

sentences.t:
τόσσος γὰρ κτύπος ἦεν, ἀϋτὴ δ’ οὐρανὸν ἷκε,
βαλλομένων σακέων τε καὶ ἱπποκόμων τρυφαλειῶν
καὶ πυλέων·
sentences.i: for the thud was so great, and the cry reached heaven, as shields and helmets with horsehair plumes and gates were struck;
sentences.n: τόσσος is ‘so great’. κτύπος and δοῦπος (289) are both ‘thud’, and ἀϋτὴ δ’ οὐρανὸν ἷκε is the stock phrase ‘and the cry reached heaven’, whose English is kept (ἀϋτή is ‘battle-cry’ elsewhere, but this phrase keeps the ‘cry’ of 2.153). The three genitives σακέων, τρυφαλειῶν and πυλέων all go with βαλλομένων ‘being struck’: ‘shields’, ‘helmets’ (τρυφάλεια, a word of unknown origin) and ‘gates’ (πύλαι, with the Ionic ending -έων). ἱπποκόμων is ‘horse-plumed’ (ἵππος + κόμη ‘hair’).

sentences.t:
πᾶσαι γὰρ ἐπώχατο, τοὶ δὲ κατ’ αὐτὰς
ἱστάμενοι πειρῶντο βίῃ ῥήξαντες ἐσελθεῖν.
sentences.l:
for all had been shut, and they, at them
taking their stand, were trying by force, having broken in, to come inside.
sentences.i: for all the gates were shut, and the Trojans, taking their stand at them, were trying to break through by force and get in.
sentences.n: ἐπώχατο is a pluperfect passive, third plural, with the old ending -ατο, ‘had been shut’; πᾶσαι is feminine and means all the gates. τοί is ‘they’, the Trojans, whom the Greek does not name. κατ’ αὐτάς is ‘at them’ with the accusative. ἱστάμενοι is ‘taking their stand’, πειρῶντο the imperfect of πειράω ‘try’, βίῃ ‘by force’, and ῥήξαντες ἐσελθεῖν ‘break in and enter’.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἐπ’ Αἴαντα προΐει κήρυκα Θοώτην·
sentences.l: And at once to Ajax he sent forth the herald Thoötes:
sentences.i: At once he sent the herald Thoötes to Ajax:
sentences.n: προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’, with ἐπί ‘to’ and the accusative. Αἴαντα is singular, ‘an Ajax’, since the next lines ask for one, or better both. κήρυκα Θοώτην is ‘the herald Thoötes’.

sentences.t:
ἔρχεο δῖε Θοῶτα, θέων Αἴαντα κάλεσσον,
ἀμφοτέρω μὲν μᾶλλον·
sentences.l:
“Go, heavenly Thoötes, running call Ajax,
both, on the one hand, rather;
sentences.i: “Go, heavenly Thoötes, run and call Ajax, or better still both of them;
sentences.n: Menestheus’ words to the herald. ἔρχεο is the imperative of ἔρχομαι, and δῖε Θοῶτα the vocative with the stock epithet δῖος ‘heavenly’. θέων is ‘running’, κάλεσσον the aorist imperative of καλέω. ἀμφοτέρω is the dual ‘both’, and μὲν … μᾶλλον ‘rather’ sets up the contrast taken up at 348 by εἰ δέ.

sentences.t:
ὃ γάρ κ’ ὄχ’ ἄριστον ἁπάντων
εἴη, ἐπεὶ τάχα τῇδε τετεύξεται αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος.
sentences.l:
for that by far the best of all
would be, since soon here steep destruction will have been prepared.
sentences.i: for that would be by far the best of all, since steep destruction will soon be prepared here.
sentences.n: ὃ is ‘that’ (neuter), the idea of calling both. ὄχ’ ἄριστον is ‘by far the best’, and κε … εἴη the potential optative. τετεύξεται is the future perfect passive of τεύχω, ‘will have been made ready’; τάχα is ‘soon’, and τῇδε ‘here’. αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος is ‘steep destruction’.

sentences.t:
ὧδε γὰρ ἔβρισαν Λυκίων ἀγοί, οἳ τὸ πάρος περ
ζαχρηεῖς τελέθουσι κατὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας.
sentences.l:
For thus have borne down the leaders of the Lycians, who as before
are very violent through the strong battles.
sentences.i: For the leaders of the Lycians have borne down so heavily, men who, as before, are very violent throughout the strong battles.
sentences.n: ὧδε ‘thus’ points to the pressure of the attack. ἔβρισαν is the aorist of βρίθω ‘bear down heavily’, ἀγοί the plural of ἀγός ‘leader’, and οἳ τὸ πάρος περ ‘who as before’. ζαχρηεῖς is ‘very violent’ (the usual sense, not certain), and τελέθουσι ‘are’; κατὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας is ‘through the strong battles’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ σφιν καὶ κεῖθι πόνος καὶ νεῖκος ὄρωρεν,
ἀλλά περ οἶος ἴτω Τελαμώνιος ἄλκιμος Αἴας,
καί οἱ Τεῦκρος ἅμα σπέσθω τόξων ἐῢ εἰδώς.
sentences.l:
But if for them there too toil and quarrel have arisen,
yet at least alone let him go, Telamonian, valiant Ajax,
and with him let Teucer follow along, well knowing the bow.”
sentences.i: But if toil and quarrel have arisen for them there too, at least let valiant Telamonian Ajax come alone, and let Teucer follow with him, who knows the bow well.”
sentences.n: εἰ δέ ‘but if’ answers the μέν of 344. σφιν is ‘for them’ and κεῖθι ‘there’; ὄρωρεν is the perfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘has arisen’. νεῖκος is ‘quarrel’, and here stands for the fighting. ἀλλά περ is ‘yet at least’, οἶος ‘alone’, and ἴτω and σπέσθω are third-person imperatives, ‘let him go’, ‘let him follow’ (σπέσθω the aorist middle of ἕπομαι). Τελαμώνιος ἄλκιμος Αἴας is ‘valiant Telamonian Ajax’; Τελαμώνιος tells him from the son of Oileus. τόξων ἐῢ εἰδώς is ‘who knows the bow well’. This ends Menestheus’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἄρα οἱ κῆρυξ ἀπίθησεν ἀκούσας,
βῆ δὲ θέειν παρὰ τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων,
στῆ δὲ παρ’ Αἰάντεσσι κιών, εἶθαρ δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, nor did the herald disobey him, having heard,
and he went to run along the wall of the bronze-shirted Achaeans,
and stood beside the Ajaxes, coming, and at once spoke to them:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the herald did not disobey him when he heard, and set off running along the wall of the bronze-shirted Achaeans and came and stood beside the Ajaxes, and at once spoke to them:
sentences.n: The first line is word for word 4.198, where it is a herald again, and its English is kept. βῆ δὲ θέειν is ‘went to run’, with the infinitive of θέω. στῆ is ἔστη without the augment, ‘stood’, and κιών is the participle of κίω ‘come’. Αἰάντεσσι is the epic dative plural, ‘the Ajaxes’. εἶθαρ is ‘at once’, and προσηύδα the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. χαλκοχιτώνων is the stock ‘bronze-shirted’.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντ’ Ἀργείων ἡγήτορε χαλκοχιτώνων
ἠνώγει Πετεῶο διοτρεφέος φίλος υἱὸς
κεῖσ’ ἴμεν, ὄφρα πόνοιο μίνυνθά περ ἀντιάσητον
ἀμφοτέρω μὲν μᾶλλον·
sentences.l:
“Ajaxes, two leaders of the bronze-shirted Argives,
bade, of Zeus-nurtured Peteos the dear son,
to go there, so that of the toil for a little while at least you two may meet,
both, on the one hand, rather;
sentences.i: “Ajaxes, you two leaders of the bronze-shirted Argives: the dear son of Zeus-nurtured Peteos has bidden you go there, so that you two may meet the toil, if only for a little while, both of you rather than one;
sentences.n: Thoötes’ words to the Ajaxes. The first line is word for word 4.285 (the speaker there is Agamemnon), where Αἴαντ’ is a vocative, as here. ἠνώγει is the pluperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, which Homer uses as a past tense (‘bade’ in l, as at 7.386); it takes the infinitive ἴμεν, and because the herald reports a command that still stands, i has ‘has bidden’. The one who bade is Menestheus, and διοτρεφέος ‘Zeus-nurtured’ agrees with Πετεῶο. κεῖσ’ is κεῖσε ‘thither’. ἀντιάσητον is the dual subjunctive of ἀντιάω ‘meet’ with the genitive πόνοιο, so the sense is ‘take their part in the toil’; μίνυνθά περ is ‘for a little while at least’. The words repeat Menestheus’ message almost exactly.

sentences.t:
ὃ γάρ κ’ ὄχ’ ἄριστον ἁπάντων
εἴη, ἐπεὶ τάχα κεῖθι τετεύξεται αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος·
sentences.l:
for that by far the best of all
would be, since soon there steep destruction will have been prepared;
sentences.i: for that would be by far the best of all, since steep destruction will soon be prepared there;
sentences.n: These words are 344–345 again, with κεῖθι ‘there’ for τῇδε ‘here’, since the herald speaks from the Ajaxes’ side. Messengers in Homer repeat their message in the words they were given.

sentences.t:
ὧδε γὰρ ἔβρισαν Λυκίων ἀγοί, οἳ τὸ πάρος περ
ζαχρηεῖς τελέθουσι κατὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας.
sentences.l:
For thus have borne down the leaders of the Lycians, who as before
are very violent through the strong battles.
sentences.i: For the leaders of the Lycians have borne down so heavily, men who, as before, are very violent throughout the strong battles.
sentences.n: These two lines are 346–347 word for word, and their English is the same.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐνθάδε περ πόλεμος καὶ νεῖκος ὄρωρεν,
ἀλλά περ οἶος ἴτω Τελαμώνιος ἄλκιμος Αἴας,
καί οἱ Τεῦκρος ἅμα σπέσθω τόξων ἐῢ εἰδώς.
sentences.l:
But if even here war and quarrel have arisen,
yet at least alone let him go, Telamonian, valiant Ajax,
and with him let Teucer follow along, well knowing the bow.”
sentences.i: But if war and quarrel have arisen even here, at least let valiant Telamonian Ajax come alone, and let Teucer follow with him, who knows the bow well.”
sentences.n: The first line differs from 348 (εἰ δέ σφιν καὶ κεῖθι πόνος …): ἐνθάδε περ ‘even here’ and πόλεμος ‘war’ stand where Menestheus had σφιν καὶ κεῖθι ‘for them there’ and πόνος ‘toil’. The other two lines are 349–350 word for word. This ends Thoötes’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, great Telamonian Ajax.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and great Telamonian Ajax did not disobey.
sentences.n: The usual ‘did not disobey’ line, with a new name. μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας is ‘great Telamonian Ajax’; Τελαμώνιος, ‘son of Telamon’, keeps him apart from the son of Oileus.

sentences.t: αὐτίκ’ Ὀϊλιάδην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: At once to Oileus’-son winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: At once he spoke winged words to the son of Oileus:
sentences.n: A whole-line speech introduction, the same as αὐτίκ’ Ἀθηναίην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα at 4.69 with a new name. Ὀϊλιάδην is the patronymic ‘son of Oileus’, the lesser Ajax. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock ‘spoke winged words’.

sentences.t:
Αἶαν σφῶϊ μὲν αὖθι, σὺ καὶ κρατερὸς Λυκομήδης,
ἑσταότες Δαναοὺς ὀτρύνετον ἶφι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
“Ajax, you two, on the one hand, here, you and strong Lycomedes,
standing, urge on the Danaans to fight with force;
sentences.i: “Ajax, you two stand here, you and strong Lycomedes, and urge the Danaans to fight powerfully;
sentences.n: Ajax son of Telamon speaks to the son of Oileus. Αἶαν is the vocative of Αἴας; σφῶϊ is the dual ‘you two’, and αὖθι ‘here’. The second member of the pair is Lycomedes. ἑσταότες is the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, and ὀτρύνετον the dual imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. ἶφι μάχεσθαι is ‘to fight with force’. Δαναούς is ‘Danaans’. κρατερός is ‘strong’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ κεῖσ’ εἶμι καὶ ἀντιόω πολέμοιο·
sentences.l: but I shall go there and meet the war;
sentences.i: but I shall go there and meet the war;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ answers the μέν of 366. εἶμι is ‘I shall go’, and κεῖσ’ ‘there’ (as at 356). ἀντιόω is the epic -ο- form of ἀντιάω ‘meet’, with the genitive πολέμοιο, ‘meet the war’, which means to take part in it.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἐλεύσομαι αὖτις, ἐπὴν εὖ τοῖς ἐπαμύνω.
sentences.l: and soon I shall come again, when well I have come to the defence of them.”
sentences.i: and I shall soon be back, once I have come properly to their defence.”
sentences.n: αἶψα is ‘soon’, ἐλεύσομαι the future of ἔρχομαι, and αὖτις ‘again, back’. ἐπήν (ἐπεὶ ἄν) takes the subjunctive ἐπαμύνω, ‘come to the defence of’, with the dative τοῖς ‘them’, the men at Menestheus’ tower. This closes Ajax’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη Τελαμώνιος Αἴας,
καί οἱ Τεῦκρος ἅμ’ ᾖε κασίγνητος καὶ ὄπατρος·
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, went away Telamonian Ajax,
and with him Teucer went along, his brother and born of the same father;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Telamonian Ajax went off, and with him went Teucer, his brother, born of the same father;
sentences.n: The first line is the usual ‘so then, having spoken, he went away’ with Ajax’s name. ἀπέβη is the aorist of ἀποβαίνω, and φωνήσας ‘having spoken’. καί οἱ is ‘and with him’; ᾖε is the imperfect of εἶμι, ‘was going’. κασίγνητος καὶ ὄπατρος is ‘brother and born of the same father’; ὄπατρος names only the shared father.

sentences.t: τοῖς δ’ ἅμα Πανδίων Τεύκρου φέρε καμπύλα τόξα.
sentences.l: and along with them Pandion bore the bent bow of Teucer.
sentences.i: and along with them Pandion carried Teucer’s bent bow.
sentences.n: τοῖς δ’ ἅμα is ‘and along with them’. Πανδίων is a man named only here, who carries Teucer’s bow. φέρε is the imperfect of φέρω without augment, ‘was carrying’. καμπύλα τόξα is ‘the bent bow’, the plural standing for a single bow, as often in Homer.

sentences.t:
εὖτε Μενεσθῆος μεγαθύμου πύργον ἵκοντο
τείχεος ἐντὸς ἰόντες, ἐπειγομένοισι δ’ ἵκοντο,
οἳ δ’ ἐπ’ ἐπάλξεις βαῖνον ἐρεμνῇ λαίλαπι ἶσοι
ἴφθιμοι Λυκίων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες·
sentences.l:
When of great-hearted Menestheus the tower they reached,
inside the wall going, to men hard-pressed they came,
and they were going up onto the battlements, like a dusky squall,
the mighty ones, the leaders of the Lycians and the lords;
sentences.i: When they reached the tower of great-hearted Menestheus, going in inside the wall, they came to men hard pressed; and they, the mighty leaders and lords of the Lycians, were climbing onto the battlements like a dusky squall;
sentences.n: εὖτε is ‘when’, with the aorist ἵκοντο ‘reached’ (without augment, as is βαῖνον later). Μενεσθῆος is the epic genitive of Μενεσθεύς, and μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ is his stock epithet. τείχεος ἐντὸς ἰόντες is ‘going inside the wall’. ἐπειγομένοισι is the dative plural of the participle of ἐπείγομαι, ‘hard pressed’: the men of the tower. οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the Lycians, and ἴφθιμοι … ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες (‘mighty’, ‘leaders and lords’) names them. ἐρεμνῇ λαίλαπι ἶσοι is ‘like a dusky squall’.

sentences.t: σὺν δ’ ἐβάλοντο μάχεσθαι ἐναντίον, ὦρτο δ’ ἀϋτή.
sentences.l: and together they set themselves to fight opposed, and the battle-cry arose.
sentences.i: and they joined together to fight opposite one another, and the battle-cry arose.
sentences.n: σὺν δ’ ἐβάλοντο is συνεβάλοντο split by tmesis: the middle of συμβάλλω, ‘they joined’, with μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ for the aim. ἐναντίον is ‘opposite’. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘arose’, and ἀϋτή is the ‘battle-cry’. The part ends with the two sides closed at Menestheus’ tower.
